en: The Philippine eagle, our national bird, has a specialized beak with a sharp, hook-like upper mandible designed to tear the flesh of its forest prey.
The Sampaguita, our national flower, releases its strong sweet fragrance at night to attract pollinating hawkmoths in the dark.
The Narra, the national tree, drops its compound leaves during the dry season to conserve water before growing new ones in the wet season.
The Ifugao built the Banaue Rice Terraces using ancient stone-walling techniques that prevent soil erosion during heavy mountain rains.
During the Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate homes with colorful kiping, which are leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice dyed with natural plant extracts.
The black sand beaches of Zambales form from magnetite and iron-rich minerals eroded from the volcanic rocks of Mount Pinatubo.
Marine biologist Angel Alcala observed that coral reefs recover faster when fishers use coral transplantation instead of destructive dynamite fishing.
The Carabao, our national animal, lacks functional sweat glands, so it wallows in mud to cool its body temperature during hot afternoons.
The giant lanterns of the San Fernando festival use hundreds of rotating, mirror-lined reflectors to direct and multiply light from bare bulbs.
The Mangyan people weave baskets from nito ferns, which thrive in the shaded, moist understory of their primary dipterocarp forests.
The underground river in Puerto Princesa flows directly into the sea, creating a unique tidal estuary where freshwater and saltwater visibly mix.
The Bangus, our national fish, survives in both freshwater lakes and saltwater seas because its gills osmoregulate to balance internal salts.
